name: Inversion table

card.summary: A tilting frame for hanging upside down, used for back traction and by height-curious forum users; any height change is described as temporary and reports of serious injury exist.
card.note: Case reports describe spinal cord injury and retinal detachment; contraindicated in several conditions.

quick.overview:
An inversion table is a frame that secures the legs and tilts the user toward or fully upside down. It is sold for back pain relief through spinal traction, and some looksmax.org users discuss it for 'heightmaxxing'.

Forum posters describe any gain as morning height that returns during the day, and some propose pairing it with glucosamine to keep it. No published trial of it for increasing adult height was found; reviews of inversion therapy describe benefits for back pain as short-term.
quick.mechanism: Body weight in the inverted position is said to create a distraction force that slightly and temporarily widens the spaces between vertebrae, similar in principle to clinical traction. Studies in healthy volunteers have measured effects of tilting on swallowing pressures, blood flow and intracranial pressure.
quick.risks: Case reports describe cervical spinal cord injury after falls from inversion tables, bilateral retinal detachment, and subdural hematomas in a person with a clotting disorder. Reference sources list heart disease, high blood pressure, glaucoma and pregnancy among conditions with higher risk, and recommend short sessions.

lead: An inversion table is a device that secures the legs and tilts the user partly or fully upside down. It is a tool of inversion therapy, a form of spinal traction in which the body hangs at an inverted angle; gravity boots are another device used for this [1].

Proponents say body weight in the inverted position distracts the spine, slightly and temporarily increasing the spacing between vertebrae and possibly reducing pressure on nerve roots [1]. Wikipedia reports that the benefit is mainly short-term, that most people see no improvement in speed or quality of recovery, and that sessions are advised to be short [1].

On looksmax.org, some users discuss inversion tables as a possible height method, while others dismiss gains as spinal decompression that reverses [2][3]. Case reports and small physiological studies address risks and effects, but no trial of height gain was found.
infobox: Back pain relief; temporary spinal decompression
Falls, retinal detachment, raised intracranial pressure

paras: Inversion tables use straps to secure the legs and then tilt the user upside down, whereas gravity boots hook onto a pull-up bar or doorway frame [1]. A 2023 article on inversion table therapy offers recommendations for its use [4].

Wikipedia states that the main benefit of inversion is short-term and that it usually feels pleasant within a few minutes [1]. The proposed mechanism is a distractive force on the spine akin to traction, which may promote muscle relaxation [1].

A looksmax.org thread cites one person who reportedly gained about two inches of morning height after ten days of inversion, with the gain fading by evening; the poster asked whether glucosamine sulphate might preserve it [2]. A reply in that thread called the loss of height through the day a 'cope', and another thread's reply described inversion as only decompressing the spine [2][3].

Wikipedia lists heart disease, high blood pressure, eye diseases such as glaucoma, and pregnancy as conditions with higher risk, notes that acid reflux in the inverted position can be dangerous, and suggests sessions of no more than about ten minutes [1].

Published case reports include three cases of cervical spinal cord injury from falls from inversion tables [5], a further case of central cord syndrome after such a fall [6], bilateral retinal detachments associated with inversion therapy [7], and bilateral subdural hematomas in an adult with hereditary factor VII deficiency, in which inversion and sit-ups were considered possible contributors [8].

No studies found of inversion tables for increasing adult height. Small physiological studies in healthy volunteers have examined what tilting does to the body. One measured optic nerve sheath diameter, heart rate, blood pressure and cerebral blood flow during inversion, using ultrasonography [9]. Another used high-resolution manometry in ten healthy adults at several tilt angles to study pharyngeal swallowing pressures [10]. A study of 18 volunteers compared tibial bone microvascular flow with artery flow during graded head-down tilt [11].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, inversion tables come up in height-focused threads, where some users report morning height gains and others regard them as temporary [2][3].

claims.claim: Using an inversion table can add inches of height.
claims.believers: A poster described someone reportedly going from 5'10 to 6'0 after ten days of inversion, though only in morning height, and said they were considering buying a cheap table to try it [2].
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes a temporary increase in spacing between vertebrae and mainly short-term benefit [1]. No published trial has tested inversion for permanent height increase.

claims.claim: Glucosamine could lock in the height gained from inversion.
claims.believers: A poster proposed that glucosamine sulphate would 'keep the morning height gains' and that months of use might add up [2].
claims.experts: No published studies were found testing glucosamine combined with inversion for height.

claims.claim: Inversion is safe for everyone to try.
claims.believers: Forum threads treat buying a cheap table as a low-stakes experiment [2].
claims.experts: Case reports describe spinal cord injury, retinal detachment and subdural hematoma, and Wikipedia lists contraindications including heart disease, hypertension, glaucoma and pregnancy [1][5][7][8].
